items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Le Chatelier’s principle"?
options: How far a reaction has proceeded towards products, measured by the change in amount of a species
An equilibrium in which all reactants and products are in the same phase
If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially counteract (minimise) the change
The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium
items.answer: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially counteract (minimise) the change

items.stem: How is the lithium-ion battery classified?
options: an electrolytic cell – needs an external power supply to operate
a fuel cell – reactants supplied continuously
items.markingKey: B. lithium-ion battery: negative electrode lithium in graphite, positive electrode lithium metal oxide (e.g. LiCoO₂).

The 1987 international agreement to phase out the production of ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs

items.stem:
Rafael studied the dissociation of colourless dinitrogen tetroxide into brown nitrogen dioxide: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). Values of Kc were measured at several temperatures.

T / K | Kc / mol dm⁻³
298 | 0.00460
323 | 0.0275
348 | 0.127
398 | 1.52

(a) Write the expression for Kc. [1]
(b) Deduce, with a reason, the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction. [2]
(c) At 323 K the equilibrium concentration of N₂O₄ is 0.084 mol dm⁻³. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of NO₂. [2]
(d) State the effect of a catalyst on the value of Kc. [1]
(e) Predict the colour change when the equilibrium mixture is placed in ice water. [2]
(f) Explain why Kc has units of mol dm⁻³ for this reaction. [1]
items.answer: (a) Kc = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] (b) positive (endothermic): Kc increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is favoured by heating. (c) 0.048 mol dm⁻³ (d) No effect – a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally. (e) It becomes paler: the exothermic reverse reaction is favoured, forming colourless N₂O₄. (f) There is one more concentration term in the numerator than the denominator: (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] correct expression (1). (b) [2] positive (1); Kc rises with T (1). (c) [2] [NO₂] = √(Kc × [N₂O₄]) = √(0.0275 × 0.084) (M1) = 0.048 mol dm⁻³ (A1). (d) [1] no change (1). (e) [2] paler (1); shift left (1). (f) [1] unit analysis (1).

items.stem:
A student made a series of buffers from 0.100 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of its sodium salt in different volume ratios and measured the pH of each with a calibrated pH meter (±0.01).

[A⁻]/[HA] | log([A⁻]/[HA]) | pH
0.25 | −0.60 | 4.27
0.50 | −0.30 | 4.55
1.00 | 0.00 | 4.89
2.00 | 0.30 | 5.18
4.00 | 0.60 | 5.46

(a) State the relationship that predicts a straight-line graph of pH against log([A⁻]/[HA]), and the expected gradient. [2]
(b) Determine the gradient from the first and last data points and comment on it. [2]
(c) Deduce the pKa of propanoic acid from the data. [1]
(d) The data-booklet pKa is 4.87. Calculate the percentage error in the student’s value. [1]
(e) Explain why diluting each buffer tenfold would have little effect on the results. [2]
(f) Suggest why the pH meter was rinsed with distilled water between readings. [1]
items.answer: (a) pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); gradient = 1 (b) 0.99 – close to the theoretical value of 1 (c) 4.89 (y-intercept, where the ratio is 1) (d) 0.4 % (e) The ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is unchanged by dilution, so the pH remains almost the same. (f) To avoid carrying over solution that would change the next buffer’s composition.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Henderson–Hasselbalch (1); gradient 1 (1). (b) [2] (5.46 − 4.27)/(0.60 − (−0.60)) = 0.99 (A1); ≈ 1, supports model (R1). (c) [1] pKa = pH when log ratio = 0: 4.89 (A1). (d) [1] |4.89 − 4.87|/4.87 × 100 = 0.4 % (A1). (e) [2] Ratio constant (1); pH depends on ratio (1). (f) [1] Prevents cross-contamination (1).

items.stem:
This question is about measuring rates of reaction and rate graphs.

(a) Which reaction could be followed using colorimetry? [2]

(b) "The rate of reaction is constant until the reaction stops." Explain the flaw in this statement. [4]

(c) Suggest a suitable method to follow the reaction Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). [4]

(d) "Initial rates are more useful than mean rates." To what extent is this view justified? [5]
items.answer: (a) the reaction of propanone with iodine (b) For most reactions the rate falls continuously as the reactant concentrations decrease. (c) Collect H₂ in a gas syringe and record volume at regular time intervals (or mass loss is too small for H₂). (d) Initial rates are essential for kinetic analysis, though mean rates are fine for simple comparisons.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] the reaction of propanone with iodine. Iodine is coloured. (b) [4 marks] For most reactions the rate falls continuously as the reactant concentrations decrease. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [4 marks] Collect H₂ in a gas syringe and record volume at regular time intervals (or mass loss is too small for H₂). (d) [5 marks] Arguments for: initial rate relates directly to known starting concentrations, so it is used to find orders; not affected by product build-up or reverse reaction. Arguments against: drawing a tangent introduces uncertainty; mean rates are easier to measure and adequate for comparisons. This question is about le Chatelier's principle and the effect of changes on position of equilibrium and K.

(a) State what is meant by the term "Le Chatelier’s principle". [2]

(b) Explain why changing the concentration of a reactant does not change Kc. [3]

(c) "Increasing the temperature always shifts the equilibrium to the right." Explain the flaw in this statement. [5]
items.answer: (a) If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially counteract (minimise) the change (b) The system responds by changing the other concentrations until the ratio in the equilibrium expression again equals Kc, which depends only on temperature. (c) Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, which may be either forward or reverse.
